title: The sisters' songs, four
tomorrow: a princess is promised to a king. what does she do with her hair?

cards: Someone says no, and the other person hears try again. It happens in hallways, in DMs, at parties. Subha is a nun walking alone to a mango grove when a man steps into her path and won't let her pass.
A gentle note for parents: her answer is startling. He praises her, and above all her eyes. She asks him what an eye even is.
Then she takes one out and hands it to him.

teach.b: Her song is long, and most of it is talk. He offers silks, jewels, a soft life; he says her eyes are like a doe's.

teach.h: A BALL IN A HOLLOW, A BUBBLE.
teach.b: She answers, in paraphrase: an eye is a little ball in a hollow, a bubble with tears and grit in it. You're in love with a painted thing.
And when he still won't move, she gives him the eye: here, take it. His wanting drops away at once. He begs her pardon.

The poem says that when she came before the Buddha, her eye was whole again. That's the week's last hard lesson: she refused, and kept refusing, and his flattery bought nothing. Now look back down the road we walked.

teach.h: SIX LINES FROM TEACHERS WHO SANG.
teach.b: A song in a cave. All things pass. As long as space remains.
The lamp goes out. So it was. Six lines from teachers who sang.

how: Subha's poem is read in Theravada teaching on desire and on seeing the body clearly; it's also read today as the story of a woman whose refusal stands.

o: poems of the early nuns, here one who refuses a man
love poems nuns wrote before they left home
the Buddha's advice to nuns on safe travel

games.q: Subha on the road — tap the pairs.
p: blocks her path to the grove
a ball in a hollow, a bubble

s: the poem treats the man's praise as a compliment she should accept
she refuses every offer, and his flattery buys nothing.
in the poem, Subha's eye is whole again when she meets the Buddha
the poem ends with her eye restored.
Subha's song is mostly her talking back to him
most of the long poem is their exchange: his offers and her answers.

games.q: a guy in your class keeps asking for your number after you said no. 'just being nice,' he says. what would Subha do?
o: say no again, plainly, and tell a trusted adult if it keeps going
give it to him once so he'll finally stop asking
laugh it off so nobody feels awkward about it
games.why: Subha refused and kept refusing; flattery bought nothing. a clear no isn't harsh, and someone who won't hear it is someone an adult should know about.

practice: Bring to mind one no that mattered: one you said and held to, or one someone said to you that turned out right. Sit with it for the whole sit, and give that refusal the respect of your full attention.

wordCard.voice: The sisters' songs, today Subha's: a nun who answers flattery with a question and a refusal no one can bargain with.

orig.note: Pali: eye. Subha asks what this praised thing really is.

carryVoice: What is an eye: Subha asked it, and the man stepped aside. The week, gathered.
